Get started with inshape

Source: vignettes/inshape.Rmd
inshape.Rmd

Register microdata comes in a few shapes: one row per unit, one row per unit and period (a panel), or one row per spell with a start and an end. Every analysis assumes the shape is right, and the errors that break it are silent: a duplicated key multiplies rows in a join, a missing year looks like an exit, an overlapping spell gives a person two addresses at once.

inshape checks the shape before anything is built on it, in two steps. The describe_*() functions look at the structure and judge nothing; the ensure_*() functions are checkpoints: each states one rule, warns or aborts with the rows that break it, and returns the data, so it sits in a pipeline. Most rules are about structure; ensure_none(), ensure_all() and ensure_empty() take any rule dplyr can express.

Function The rule Returns
describe_key() (look) duplicated keys, exact copies vs. conflicts a summary
describe_panel() (look) units, gaps, entries, exits, patterns a summary
describe_spells() (look) gaps, transfers, overlapping and nested spells a summary
describe_varying() (look) which columns vary within units a summary
describe_codes() (look) how the codes of a column change over periods a summary
describe_changes() (look) what changed between two extracts a summary
describe_match() (look) what a join of two tables will do a summary
ensure_codes() a coded column holds only codes from the code list the data
ensure_complete() the columns named have no missing values the data
ensure_constant() sex, birth date and the like are constant within a unit the data
ensure_unique() the key columns identify each row the data
ensure_balanced() every unit is observed in every period, or has no gaps the data
ensure_no_overlap() a unit’s spells do not overlap the data
ensure_no_gaps() a unit’s spells leave no gaps between them the data
ensure_within() no rows after death or emigration, or before birth the data
ensure_valid_spells() a spell has a start and does not end before it the data
ensure_matched() every key occurs in a reference register the data
ensure_panel() the key is complete and unique, and no unit skips a period the data
ensure_spells() the unit is complete, the spells valid and not overlapping the data
ensure_lookup() a lookup table’s key is unique and covers the data the data
describe_groups() (look) the compositions of groups such as families a summary
ensure_counts() rows of each role per group within limits the data
ensure_references() a row pointing to another finds it, and agrees the data
describe_events() (look) events per unit, per period, and the time between a summary
ensure_sequence() one event comes before another the data
ensure_reconciled() microdata give the numbers of a published table the data
ensure_stock_flow() a stock is the stock before plus its flows the data
ensure_none() no row matches a condition (NA passes) the data
ensure_all() every row meets a condition (NA fails) the data
ensure_empty() a violation set you built yourself has no rows the set
tally_violations() (count) violations for many rules at once a tally
describe_transitions() (look) how a status changes from one observation to the next a summary
ensure_transitions() a status does not change in a forbidden way the data
merge_spells() (fix) spells recorded as several, merged merged spells
fill_panel() (fix) missing unit-periods added as rows the filled panel
carry_status() (fix) a status that holds once reached, carried forward the data plus status
spells_to_panel() (conversion) spells to a period panel a panel
add_spell_status() (conversion) status from spells on an existing panel the data plus status

Look first: describe_panel() and describe_key()

A rule is easier to choose when you have seen the data. describe_panel() summarises a panel in one pass: how many units are observed throughout, who enters and leaves when, where the gaps are, and which participation patterns are common, as Stata’s xtdescribe does.

persons <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "d", "d", "d", "d"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2022)
)

describe_panel(persons, cpr, year)
#> ── Panel: cpr by year ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 10 rows, 4 units, 3 periods, 2020-2022
#> 
#> ⚠ With gaps: 1 unit (25.0%), 1 missing unit-period inside their span
#> ⚠ Duplicated unit-periods: 1 (1 extra row)
#> • Observed in every period: 2 units (50.0%)
#> 
#> By period:
#>     period units entries exits  gaps
#>   1   2020     3      NA     0     0
#>   2   2021     2       0     0     1
#>   3   2022     4       1    NA     0
#> 
#> Most common patterns:
#>     pattern units share
#>   1 111         2 50.0%
#>   2 1.1         1 25.0%
#>   3 ..1         1 25.0%

A period with no units, or a sudden fall in units, is the sign of a broken extract. The counts are there to use as well, e.g. describe_panel(persons, cpr, year)$by_period.

describe_key() looks at a key. When it is not unique, the question is what the duplicates are: exact copies, which can be dropped, or rows that disagree, which need a rule. It tells them apart and names the columns the copies disagree in:

firms <- tibble(
  cvr      = c("1", "1", "2", "2", "3"),
  year     = 2024,
  industry = c("A", "A", "B", "C", "A")
)

describe_key(firms, cvr, year)
#> ── Key: cvr, year ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 5 rows, 3 distinct keys
#> 
#> ⚠ Duplicated keys: 2 (4 rows, 2 extra rows)
#> ⚠ Copies differ in: industry (1)
#> • Exact copies, identical in every column: 1 of 2 keys
#> • Copies per duplicated key: 2 (2)

Keys: ensure_unique()

Duplicate keys are the most common error in register data, and the most costly one sits right before a join. A lookup table with a duplicated key makes left_join() multiply rows without a word. Check the key first:

df <- tibble(
  cvr  = c("11111111", "22222222", "11111111"),
  year = c(2024, 2024, 2024)
)

df |>
  ensure_unique(cvr, year, warn_msg = "Duplicate company-years")
#> Warning in ensure_unique(df, cvr, year, warn_msg = "Duplicate company-years"): Duplicate company-years
#> ℹ 2 rows in 1 group
#>   The copies are identical in every column
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     dupid cvr       year
#>     <int> <chr>    <dbl>
#>   1     1 11111111  2024
#>   2     1 11111111  2024
#> ℹ To drop the exact copies: dplyr::distinct(df)

The reported rows carry a dupid, so the copies in each group sit together.

Every failure is laid out the same way: what broke, how many rows, counts that show the pattern, the first rows, and the next step as code to copy. Here some duplicates are exact copies and one person has two municipalities in the same year:

persons_2019 <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c", "d"),
  year = c(2019, 2019, 2019, 2019, 2021, 2021, 2021),
  kom  = c("955", "955", "955", "956", "957", "957", "955")
)

ensure_unique(persons_2019, cpr, year)
#> Warning in ensure_unique(persons_2019, cpr, year): Duplicate rows on cpr, year
#> ℹ 6 rows in 3 groups
#>   2 groups are exact copies
#>   1 group differs in: kom (1)
#>   By year: 2019 (4), 2021 (2)
#> ℹ The first 5 rows:
#>     dupid cpr    year kom
#>     <int> <chr> <dbl> <chr>
#>   1     1 a      2019 955
#>   2     1 a      2019 955
#>   3     2 b      2019 955
#>   4     2 b      2019 956
#>   5     3 c      2021 957
#>   # ℹ 1 more row
#> ℹ For all rows: violations(ensure_unique(persons_2019, cpr, year))
#> ℹ To drop the exact copies: dplyr::distinct(persons_2019)
#> ℹ Copies that differ need a rule for which to keep, e.g. dplyr::slice_max(persons_2019, <column>, by = c(cpr, year))

The hints never choose for you. Exact copies can only be dropped one way, so the hint is the code; copies that differ need a rule for which to keep, so the code has a hole, <column>, for you to fill.

Missing values: ensure_complete()

Some columns an analysis cannot do without: the id, the date, the outcome. A missing value in them drops the row from a model without a word, or becomes a group of its own in a count. ensure_complete() requires the columns named to have a value in every row, or all columns if none are named. The reported rows carry a missing column that names the columns missing in each:

register <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "b", NA, "d"),
  born = as.Date(c("1980-05-01", NA, NA, "1975-02-11")),
  sex  = c("F", "M", "F", NA)
)

ensure_complete(register, cpr, born)
#> Warning in ensure_complete(register, cpr, born): Missing values in: cpr, born
#> ℹ 2 rows in 2 groups
#>   Missing per column: born (2), cpr (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     missing   cpr   born   sex
#>     <chr>     <chr> <date> <chr>
#>   1 born      b     NA     M
#>   2 cpr, born NA    NA     F

Missing means NA; an empty string is a value.

Panels: ensure_balanced()

A yearly register extract is a panel: one row per person (or company) and year. Whether it is balanced, every unit present in every year, decides which methods are valid and often reveals a broken extract.

panel <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022)
)

ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year)
#> Warning in ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year): Panel is not balanced: missing cpr-year combinations
#> ℹ 3 rows
#>   Missing for 2 units
#>   By year: 2021 (2), 2020 (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     cpr    year
#>     <chr> <dbl>
#>   1 b      2021
#>   2 c      2020
#>   3 c      2021
#> ℹ If units may enter late and leave early: ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE)
#> ℹ To add them as rows with missing values: fill_panel(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = FALSE)

Real populations are rarely balanced. People are born, die and migrate. What usually should hold is that a unit, once present, does not skip a year before it leaves. gaps_only = TRUE checks that: c entering in 2022 is fine, b missing in 2021 is not.

ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE)
#> Warning in ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE): Gaps in panel: missing cpr-year combinations
#> ℹ 1 row
#>   Missing for 1 unit
#>   By year: 2021 (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     cpr    year
#>     <chr> <dbl>
#>   1 b      2021
#> ℹ To add them as rows with missing values: fill_panel(panel, cpr, year)

By default the expected years are those found in the data, so a year that was never loaded goes unnoticed. State the years you expect to catch that as well:

ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, periods = 2015:2024, gaps_only = TRUE)

When the gaps are real, fill_panel() adds them as rows with the unit and the period filled in and everything else missing, so a count per year sees them. It says how many rows it added:

filled <- fill_panel(panel, cpr, year)
#> ℹ Added 1 row for 1 unit, with every column but cpr, year missing.

Status over time: describe_transitions(), ensure_transitions() and carry_status()

A status that follows a person, such as education, can only change in some ways. describe_transitions() counts the units going from each status to each other between two observations, so the impossible ones show as cells that should be empty:

education <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"),
  year   = c(2019, 2020, 2021, 2019, 2020, 2019, 2021),
  status = c("not started", "enrolled", "completed",
             "enrolled", "completed", "completed", "not started")
)

describe_transitions(education, cpr, year, status)
#> ── Transitions: status by year per cpr ─────────────────────────────────────────
#> 7 rows, 3 units, 4 pairs of consecutive observations
#> 
#> • Changing status: 4 of 4 pairs (100.0%)
#> 
#> Units per transition, from (rows) to (columns):
#>   from \ to   completed  enrolled  not started
#>   completed            0         0            1
#>   enrolled             2         0            0
#>   not started          0         1            0

ensure_transitions() forbids them, as pairs or as a final status nothing may follow:

ensure_transitions(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed")
#> Warning in ensure_transitions(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed"): Forbidden transitions: status by year per cpr
#> ℹ 1 row in 1 group
#>   In 1 unit
#>   By transition: completed -> not started (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     transition               cpr   previous  year status
#>     <chr>                    <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#>   1 completed -> not started c         2019  2021 not started
#> ℹ If the final status is right and the later ones wrong: carry_status(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed")

Which of the two observations is wrong, the package cannot know. When you know that the final status holds, carry_status() carries it forward, into a new column so the original stands beside it, and counts what it changed:

education <- carry_status(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed")
#> ℹ Changed 1 row in 1 unit:
#>   not started -> completed: 1 row in 1 unit

The unit is what id says: when a person may complete one education and start another, use id = c(cpr, education).

Spells: ensure_no_overlap()

The other shape of register data is spells: address periods, employment, benefit periods. A person has only one address at a time, so overlapping spells within a person are an error:

addresses <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2020-06-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-12-31", NA,           "2020-06-30", "2021-12-31"))
)

ensure_no_overlap(addresses, cpr, start, end)
#> Warning in ensure_no_overlap(addresses, cpr, start, end): Overlapping spells per cpr
#> ℹ 2 rows in 1 group
#>   In 1 unit
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     overlap_id cpr   start      end
#>          <int> <chr> <date>     <date>
#>   1          1 b     2020-01-01 2020-06-30
#>   2          1 b     2020-06-01 2021-12-31
#> ℹ If they are one spell recorded more than once: merge_spells(addresses, cpr, start, end)

Spells are closed intervals, and a missing end means the spell is ongoing. The reported rows carry an overlap_id that groups spells overlapping each other, the same idea as dupid.

The opposite rule is ensure_no_gaps(): where a person must have an address every day, a spell that starts later than the day after the earlier ones ended leaves days without one. The spell after each gap is reported with the length of the gap, and max_gap accepts short ones:

moves <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2020-07-04")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-12-31", NA,           "2020-06-30", "2021-12-31"))
)

ensure_no_gaps(moves, cpr, start, end)
#> Warning in ensure_no_gaps(moves, cpr, start, end): Gaps between spells per cpr
#> ℹ 1 row
#>   In 1 unit
#>   Gap length: shortest 3, median 3, longest 3
#> ℹ The rows:
#>       gap cpr   start      end
#>     <int> <chr> <date>     <date>
#>   1     3 b     2020-07-04 2021-12-31
#> ℹ To join spells across gaps up to a length you choose: merge_spells(moves, cpr, start, end, max_gap = <length>)

Before requiring that, look at how the spells relate to each other. describe_spells() takes each unit’s spells in order and says, for each, how it relates to the earlier ones: after a gap, adjacent (starting the day after one ends, often a transfer recorded as two spells), touching on one shared day, overlapping, nested or a duplicate. In patient registers up to a quarter of the entries can be such transfers, and counting spells without merging them first inflates every count.

admissions <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2020-01-11", "2020-03-01",
                    "2020-01-01", "2020-01-05", "2021-06-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-01-10", "2020-01-20", "2020-03-05",
                    "2020-01-31", "2020-01-10", NA))
)

describe_spells(admissions, cpr, start, end)
#> ── Spells: start to end per cpr ────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 6 rows, 6 usable spells, 3 units
#> 
#> ✔ Every spell has a start and ends after it
#> ⚠ Units with overlapping spells: 1 (33.3%)
#> • Ongoing (no end): 1
#> 
#> Relation to the unit's earlier spells:
#>     relation    spells
#>   1 gap              1
#>   2 adjacent         1
#>   3 touching         0
#>   4 overlapping      0
#>   5 nested           1
#>   6 duplicate        0
#> 
#> Gaps between spells, in days:
#>         n   min   q25 median  mean   q75   max
#>   1     1    40    40     40    40    40    40
#> 
#> Length of ended spells, in days:
#>         n   min   q25 median  mean   q75   max
#>   1     5     5     6     10  12.4    10    31

merge_spells() merges them: by default spells that overlap or follow the next day become one, from the first start to the latest end, and n_spells counts what was merged. max_gap = 30 also merges spells less than a month apart, a readmission counted as the same episode, and by merges only spells that agree in a column such as the employer:

merge_spells(admissions, cpr, start, end)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   cpr   start      end        n_spells
#>   <chr> <date>     <date>        <int>
#> 1 a     2020-01-01 2020-01-20        2
#> 2 a     2020-03-01 2020-03-05        1
#> 3 b     2020-01-01 2020-01-31        2
#> 4 c     2021-06-01 NA                1

Attributes of the unit: describe_varying() and ensure_constant()

Sex and birth date belong to the person, not to the year, yet a panel repeats them on every row, and a person with two values is an error, usually of linkage or of a correction applied to some years only. describe_varying() shows which columns vary within units, from the constant to the varying. A column that varies for a handful of units out of millions is rarely meant to vary:

persons <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"),
  year   = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2021, 2020, 2021),
  sex    = c("F", "F", "M", "F", "M", NA),
  income = c(100, 120, 90, 95, 80, 85)
)

describe_varying(persons, cpr)
#> ── Within cpr ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 3 units, 3 columns
#> 
#> ✔ No column is nearly constant
#> • Constant: 0 columns
#> 
#> Per column:
#>     column varying share   partly_missing all_missing
#>   1 sex          1 33.33%               1           0
#>   2 income       3 100.00%              0           0
#>   3 year         3 100.00%              0           0

ensure_constant() turns that into a rule and lists every row of the units that break it. A missing value is not a contradiction, so c passes:

ensure_constant(persons, cpr, sex)
#> Warning in ensure_constant(persons, cpr, sex): Varies within units: sex per cpr
#> ℹ 2 rows
#>   In 1 unit
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     cpr   sex    year income
#>     <chr> <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>
#>   1 b     M      2020     90
#>   2 b     F      2021     95
#> ℹ Which value holds is a choice, e.g. dplyr::mutate(persons, sex = <first, last or most common>, .by = cpr)

Codes over time: describe_codes() and ensure_codes()

Code lists change: municipalities merge, industry codes are revised. describe_codes() shows when each code occurs, so a revision stands out as a period with many new and many gone codes, and a typo as a code seen once:

residents <- tibble(
  year = rep(2018:2021, each = 4),
  municipality = c("955", "956", "957", NA,    "955", "956", "957", "957",
                   "960", "956", "957", "95",  "960", "965", "957", "956")
)

describe_codes(residents, municipality, year)
#> ── Codes: municipality by year ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 16 rows, 6 codes, 4 periods, 2018-2021
#> 
#> ✔ No code skips a period
#> ⚠ Rows with a missing municipality: 1
#> • In every period: 2 codes (33.3%)
#> 
#> By period:
#>     period codes   new  gone missing
#>   1   2018     3    NA    NA       1
#>   2   2019     3     0     0       0
#>   3   2020     4     2     1       0
#>   4   2021     4     1     1       0
#> 
#> Codes not in every period, skipping first:
#>     code  first  last periods  gaps  rows
#>   1 95     2020  2020       1     0     1
#>   2 965    2021  2021       1     0     1
#>   3 955    2018  2019       2     0     2
#>   4 960    2020  2021       2     0     2

ensure_codes() requires the codes of a code list:

ensure_codes(residents, municipality, c("955", "956", "957", "960", "965"))
#> Warning in ensure_codes(residents, municipality, c("955", "956", "957", : Codes not in the code list: municipality
#> ℹ 1 row in 1 group
#>   Codes: 95 (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     municipality  year
#>     <chr>        <int>
#>   1 95            2020

A new extract: describe_changes()

A register is delivered again and again, and the same person-year should not change between deliveries unless it was corrected. describe_changes() compares two extracts by their key:

before <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "c"), year = 2023,
                 sex = c("F", "M", "F"), born = c(1950, 1960, NA))
after  <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "d"), year = 2023,
                 sex = c("F", "F", "M"), born = c(1950, 1960, 1990))

describe_changes(before, after, cpr, year)
#> ── Changes by cpr, year ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 3 rows before, 3 rows now, 2 keys in both
#> 
#> ✔ The same columns, with the same types
#> • New keys: 1 (33.3%)
#> • Keys gone: 1 (33.3%)
#> • Keys with a changed value: 1 (50.0%)
#> 
#> Changes per column, among the keys in both:
#>     column changed went_missing filled_in share 
#>   1 sex          1            0         0 50.00%
#>   2 born         0            0         0 0.00%

Within a lifetime: ensure_within()

Registers are updated at different times, so a linked extract can hold a person after death or emigration, or income before birth. ensure_within() requires each row to lie between its own bounds, usually joined on from the population register. A yearly row counts by the year, so the year of death itself is fine:

panel <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b"),
  year  = c(2022, 2023, 2024, 2022, 2023),
  born  = as.Date(c("1950-04-01", "1950-04-01", "1950-04-01", "2023-01-10", "2023-01-10")),
  death = as.Date(c("2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", NA, NA))
)

ensure_within(panel, year, from = born, to = death)
#> Warning in ensure_within(panel, year, from = born, to = death): Rows outside: year within born to death
#> ℹ 2 rows in 2 groups
#>   Bounds broken: after death (1), before born (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     outside      year born       death      cpr
#>     <chr>       <dbl> <date>     <date>     <chr>
#>   1 after death  2024 1950-04-01 2023-05-01 a
#>   2 before born  2022 2023-01-10 NA         b

From spells to a panel: spells_to_panel()

spells_to_panel() turns spells into one row per unit and year (or by = "quarter"/"month"), with the status at primo and ultimo. By default primo is the previous ultimo, so primo 2021 is the status on 31 December 2020.

In an education register the status is the outcome of the spell, passed or dropped out. With status_is = "outcome", a running spell shows as ongoing and the outcome applies from the end date until a new spell starts:

education <- data.frame(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b"),
  start  = as.Date(c("2018-08-15", "2021-08-15", "2019-08-15")),
  end    = as.Date(c("2021-06-20", NA,           "2020-03-01")),
  status = c("passed", "in progress", "dropped out")
)

education |>
  spells_to_panel(cpr, start, end, status,
                  from = 2018, to = 2022,
                  status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>    cpr    year primo       ultimo     
#>    <chr> <int> <chr>       <chr>      
#>  1 a      2018 NA          in progress
#>  2 a      2019 in progress in progress
#>  3 a      2020 in progress in progress
#>  4 a      2021 in progress in progress
#>  5 a      2022 in progress in progress
#>  6 b      2018 NA          NA         
#>  7 b      2019 NA          in progress
#>  8 b      2020 in progress dropped out
#>  9 b      2021 dropped out dropped out
#> 10 b      2022 dropped out dropped out

With the default status_is = "state", the status holds for the whole spell (enrolled, on leave) and is NA outside spells. from and to give every unit the same window, which makes a balanced panel.

Status on a panel you have: add_spell_status()

Often the panel exists already, and the spells should only add a status to it. A left_join(join_by(between())) does that until the data gets messy: overlapping spells duplicate rows, and an ongoing spell with no end matches nothing. add_spell_status() keeps the rows of the panel exactly as they are and uses the rules of spells_to_panel():

population <- data.frame(cpr  = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
                         year = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2020))

population |>
  add_spell_status(education, cpr, year, start, end, status,
                   status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
#>   cpr year status_primo status_ultimo
#> 1   a 2020  in progress   in progress
#> 2   a 2021  in progress   in progress
#> 3   b 2020  in progress   dropped out
#> 4   c 2020         <NA>          <NA>

Valid boundaries and reference coverage

Validate spell boundaries before checking their relationships. Missing ends represent ongoing spells; open_end = FALSE requires closed spells.

ensure_valid_spells(education, start, end)
#> ✔ Valid spells: start to end

Check that each observation can be linked to a reference register. Duplicate reference keys do not multiply rows, and missing keys do not match unless na_matches = "na" is specified.

observations <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "c"), year = 2020)
reference <- tibble(person_id = c("a", "b"), year = 2020)
ensure_matched(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", "year"))
#> Warning in ensure_matched(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", : Keys missing from the reference: cpr, year
#> ℹ 1 row found:
#>     cpr    year
#>     <chr> <dbl>
#>   1 c      2020

The common checks in one call: ensure_panel(), ensure_spells() and ensure_lookup()

A panel nearly always needs the same three checks: the key is complete, unique and without gaps. ensure_panel() runs them all, also after one has failed, and shows one overview instead of three messages, each pointing to the single check that gives the rows:

yearly <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "d", "d", "d", "d"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2022)
)

ensure_panel(yearly, cpr, year)
#> Warning in ensure_panel(yearly, cpr, year): Panel cpr by year: 2 of 3 checks failed
#> ✔ Complete: cpr, year
#> ✖ Duplicate rows on cpr, year (2 rows in 1 group)
#>   The copies are identical in every column
#> ✖ Gaps in panel: missing cpr-year combinations (1 row)
#>   Missing for 1 unit
#>   By year: 2021 (1)
#> ℹ For the rows: violations(ensure_unique(yearly, cpr, year))
#> ℹ For the rows: violations(ensure_balanced(yearly, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE))

ensure_spells() does the same for spells: the unit is complete, the spells are valid and do not overlap, and with no_gaps = TRUE leave no gaps. Overlaps mean nothing until the spells are valid, so they are not checked until then. ensure_lookup() checks a table before a join: its key is unique, so the join does not multiply rows, and every key of the data is in it.

ensure_lookup(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", "year"))
#> Warning in ensure_lookup(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", : Lookup on cpr, year: 1 of 2 checks failed
#> ✔ Unique keys in reference: person_id, year
#> ✖ Keys missing from the reference: cpr, year (1 row)
#> ℹ For the rows: violations(ensure_matched(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", "year")))

The choices are fixed where registers nearly always need the same; a panel may have late entries and early exits (gaps_only = TRUE). For anything else, run the single checks.

Before a join: describe_match()

ensure_matched() asks one question of a join, whether every row finds a match. describe_match() looks at the whole of it first: how many keys are in both tables, how many only in one, and whether the reference repeats a key, so that a left join returns more rows than it was given. Here c is not in the register, d has no income, and b is registered twice:

income <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b", "c", NA),
  year   = c(2023, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024),
  income = c(10, 12, 7, 9, 3)
)
population_register <- tibble(
  person_id = c("a", "b", "b", "d"),
  kommune   = c("955", "956", "957", "960")
)

describe_match(income, population_register, by = c(cpr = "person_id"))
#> ── Match: cpr = person_id ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> data: 5 rows, reference: 4 rows
#> 
#> ⚠ Rows of data without a match: 2 (40.0%), 1 of them with a missing key
#> ⚠ Keys repeated in the reference: 1; a left join returns 6 rows, 1 more than data
#> 
#> Keys:
#>     found              keys  rows ref_rows
#>   1 in both               2     3        3
#>   2 only in data          1     1        0
#>   3 only in reference     1     0        1

A row with a missing key matches nothing and is counted on its own. The key must be stated in by: a join on whatever names two registers happen to share is how a wrong key goes unnoticed.

Codes valid at the observation time

A temporal code list has code, valid_from and valid_to. Bounds are inclusive, missing bounds are open, and a code may have several intervals. Time and bounds use the same scale: dates, date-times, or numeric periods. Missing observation times fail for non-missing codes. na_ok controls missing codes separately.

codebook <- tibble(code = c("A", "B"),
                   valid_from = c(2015, 2020), valid_to = c(2019, NA_real_))
coded <- tibble(classification = c("A", "A", "B"), year = c(2019, 2020, 2020))
ensure_codes(coded, classification, codebook, time = year)
#> Warning in ensure_codes(coded, classification, codebook, time = year): Codes not in the code list: classification
#> ℹ 1 row in 1 group
#>   Codes: A (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     classification  year
#>     <chr>          <dbl>
#>   1 A               2020

Families and other groups: describe_groups(), ensure_counts() and ensure_references()

A family is a group of persons, each with a role in it. The rules are about how the group is composed and whether its members point to each other. Since the definition of a family differs between registers and over time, inshape has no family check built in, but three building blocks that also fit households and workplaces. describe_groups() shows the compositions there are, so the impossible ones show first:

families <- tibble(
  family = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4),
  cpr    = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h"),
  role   = c("reference", "partner", "child", "reference", "child",
             "child", "reference", "reference"),
  spouse = c("b", "a", NA, NA, NA, NA, "x", NA)
)

describe_groups(families, family, role)
#> ── Groups: family by role ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 8 rows, 4 groups, 3 roles
#> 
#> • Compositions: 4
#> 
#> Most common compositions:
#>     composition                       groups share
#>   1 1 child                                1 25.0%
#>   2 1 child + 1 partner + 1 reference      1 25.0%
#>   3 1 child + 1 reference                  1 25.0%
#>   4 2 reference                            1 25.0%

ensure_counts() states the limits per role, and ensure_references() checks that a spouse is found, points back and is in the same family:

ensure_counts(families, family, role, limits = list(reference = 1, partner = c(0, 1)))
#> Warning in ensure_counts(families, family, role, limits = list(reference = 1, : Outside the limits: role per family
#> ℹ 3 rows
#>   In 2 groups
#>   reference: 0 (needs 1) in 1 group
#>   reference: 2 (needs 1) in 1 group
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     family role      broken                 cpr   spouse
#>      <dbl> <chr>     <chr>                  <chr> <chr>
#>   1      3 child     reference: 0 (needs 1) f     NA
#>   2      4 reference reference: 2 (needs 1) g     x
#>   3      4 reference reference: 2 (needs 1) h     NA

ensure_references(families, cpr, spouse, same = family, mutual = TRUE)
#> Warning in ensure_references(families, cpr, spouse, same = family, mutual = TRUE): Broken references: spouse to cpr
#> ℹ 1 row in 1 group
#>   Problems: not found (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     problem   cpr   spouse family role
#>     <chr>     <chr> <chr>   <dbl> <chr>
#>   1 not found g     x           4 reference

Shared facts such as the family type or the address are ensure_constant(families, family, type), and a person in at most one family a year is ensure_unique(families, cpr, year).

Events: describe_events() and ensure_sequence()

Events have many rows per unit: moves, exams, contacts. describe_events() counts them per unit, per period and per type, and the time between a unit’s events; ensure_sequence() requires one event before another. Two of a kind that can happen once, such as deaths, is ensure_counts() with the event as the role.

school <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  date  = as.Date(c("2020-08-15", "2021-06-01", "2021-06-01", "2021-08-15", "2021-06-01")),
  event = c("enrolled", "exam", "exam", "enrolled", "exam")
)

ensure_sequence(school, cpr, date, event, first = "enrolled", then = "exam")
#> Warning in ensure_sequence(school, cpr, date, event, first = "enrolled", : exam before enrolled per cpr
#> ℹ 2 rows in 2 groups
#>   In 2 units
#>   Reasons: before enrolled (1), no enrolled (1)
#> ℹ The rows:
#>     reason          cpr   date       event
#>     <chr>           <chr> <date>     <chr>
#>   1 before enrolled b     2021-06-01 exam
#>   2 no enrolled     c     2021-06-01 exam

Do the numbers add up: ensure_reconciled() and ensure_stock_flow()

The shape can be right and the numbers still wrong. ensure_reconciled() counts the microdata by the dimensions of a published table and compares cell for cell. The table is a data frame you read yourself; a year read as text matches a numeric one:

residents <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e"),
  year = c(2023, 2023, 2024, 2024, 2024),
  sex  = c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M")
)
statbank <- tibble(
  tid = c("2023", "2023", "2024", "2024"),
  sex = c("F", "M", "F", "M"),
  n   = c(1, 1, 3, 1)
)

ensure_reconciled(residents, statbank, by = c(year = "tid", "sex"))
#> Warning in ensure_reconciled(residents, statbank, by = c(year = "tid", "sex")): The count differs from the table by year, sex
#> ℹ 1 row
#>   Of 4 cells compared
#>   Difference: total -1, largest -1
#> ℹ The rows:
#>      year sex    data published difference
#>     <dbl> <chr> <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
#>   1  2024 F         2         3         -1
#> ℹ If the table is rounded or perturbed for disclosure: tolerance = <largest accepted difference>

ensure_stock_flow() checks a population account: the stock at the end of a period is the stock before, plus the flows in, minus the flows out.

account <- tibble(
  year       = 2021:2024,
  population = c(56000, 56100, 56210, 56300),
  born       = c(800, 820, 790, 810),
  immigrated = c(2000, 2100, 2050, 2200),
  dead       = c(500, 520, 510, 530),
  emigrated  = c(2200, 2300, 2280, 2330)
)

ensure_stock_flow(account, year, population,
                  inflow = c(born, immigrated), outflow = c(dead, emigrated))
#> Warning in ensure_stock_flow(account, year, population, inflow = c(born, : The account does not add up: population by year
#> ℹ 2 rows
#>   Difference: total 0, largest 60
#> ℹ The rows:
#>      year population difference expected  born immigrated  dead emigrated
#>     <int>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#>   1  2023      56210         60    56150   790       2050   510      2280
#>   2  2024      56300        -60    56360   810       2200   530      2330

Rules of your own: ensure_none(), ensure_all() and ensure_empty()

The structure checks cover the rules every register has. The rest are particular to a delivery: no negative amounts, every cvr eight digits, a total that matches its parts. Any rule dplyr can express is a checkpoint, stated as “the set of violations must be empty”.

ensure_none() takes the condition for a violating row and returns the full data, so checks chain before the real work continues:

sales <- tibble(
  order_id    = 1001:1006,
  customer_id = c(12, 17, NA, 25, 31, NA),
  amount      = c(250, -40, 120, 80, -15, 300)
)

sales |>
  ensure_none(amount < 0, warn_msg = "Negative amounts") |>
  ensure_none(amount > 1e6) |>
  nrow()
#> Warning in ensure_none(sales, amount < 0, warn_msg = "Negative amounts"): Negative amounts
#> ℹ 2 rows found:
#>     order_id customer_id amount
#>        <int>       <dbl>  <dbl>
#>   1     1002          17    -40
#>   2     1005          31    -15
#> ✔ No rows where amount > 1e+06
#> [1] 6

Without a message, the condition becomes one, which is often enough at the console. Give checks that stay in a script a message in your own words. Messages are shown literally, so "cvr must match ^\\d{8}$" is safe.

The condition follows filter(): a row where it is NA is not a violation. ensure_all() states the rule positively instead, and there a row passes only when the condition is TRUE, so a missing value is a violation:

sales |>
  ensure_none(customer_id < 0)
#> ✔ No rows where customer_id < 0

sales |>
  ensure_all(customer_id > 0)
#> Warning in ensure_all(sales, customer_id > 0): Found rows that do not meet customer_id > 0
#> ℹ 2 rows found:
#>     order_id customer_id amount
#>        <int>       <dbl>  <dbl>
#>   1     1003          NA    120
#>   2     1006          NA    300

No customer id is negative, but two are missing. Use ensure_all() when a value has to be present and right, and ensure_none() when a missing value is acceptable or a rule of its own, such as ensure_complete().

ensure_empty() is the most general form: build the violation set yourself, with a filter() or an anti-join, and pipe it in.

expected |>
  dplyr::anti_join(delivery, by = "cvr") |>
  ensure_empty(warn_msg = "Firms missing from the delivery")

Many rules at once: tally_violations()

A chain of checkpoints stops at the first abort. When a delivery has five problems, you want to hear about all five in one go. tally_violations() evaluates every rule and counts the violating rows, but never warns or stops: the checkpoints judge, the tally only counts.

report <- sales |>
  tally_violations(
    "Negative amount" = amount < 0,
    "No customer"     = is.na(customer_id),
    "Huge amount"     = amount > 1e6
  )
report
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   rule                n total rows     
#>   <chr>           <int> <int> <list>   
#> 1 Negative amount     2     6 <int [2]>
#> 2 No customer         2     6 <int [2]>
#> 3 Huge amount         0     6 <int [0]>

rows holds the row numbers of each rule’s violations. Filtered to the rules that failed, the tally is itself a violation set. total is the number of rows checked, so the same tally can warn about every broken rule and stop only for those broken at scale:

report |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 0) |>
  ensure_empty(warn_msg = "Rules with violations")

report |>
  dplyr::filter(n / total > 0.001) |>
  ensure_empty(abort_msg = "Rules broken by more than 0.1 % of the rows")

Personal data and large registers

inshape is made for interactive review of registers, at the console in the environment where the data lives. The offending rows of a check are personal data, so inshape writes nothing to disk, neither rows nor a log. A failure shows the count and the first rows. Wrap the check in violations() to get all of them, to look at in the session; when the check passes, it returns no rows:

gaps <- violations(ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE))
#> ✔ No gaps in year per cpr
gaps
#> # A tibble: 0 × 4
#> # ℹ 4 variables: cpr <chr>, year <dbl>, born <date>, death <date>

Whether rows are kept anywhere is for the analysis and its data agreement to decide. To save them, do it yourself, from the rows violations() returns:

violations(ensure_none(sales, amount < 0)) |>
  data.table::fwrite("negative_amounts.csv")

A DuckDB or Arrow table is checked where it lives, and only the count and the first rows are fetched into R. See ?checkpoints for both.
